title: Yayoi Kusama
wiki_lead:
Yayoi Kusama (草間 彌生, Kusama Yayoi; 22 March 1929 – 14 August 2026) was a Japanese artist who worked primarily in sculpture and installation. She was also active in painting, performance art, video art, fashion, poetry, and fiction. Rooted in conceptual art, her work incorporates elements of feminist art, minimalism, surrealism, art brut, pop art, and abstract expressionism, and is infused with autobiographical, psychological, and sexual themes. Acknowledged as one of the most important artists to emerge from Japan, she was among the world's top-selling female artists, ranking 19th on Sotheby's 2023 list of the top 50 artists. Her work influenced her contemporaries, including Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg.
Raised in Matsumoto, Kusama trained for a year at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts in the traditional Japanese painting style nihonga. Drawn to European and American avant-garde movements—particularly abstract expressionism—she moved to New York City in 1958 and was a part of the New York avant-garde scene throughout the 1960s, especially in the pop art movement. Embracing the rise of the hippie counterculture of the late 1960s, she came to public attention when she organized a series of happenings in which nude participants were painted with brightly colored polka dots. Although her work was largely overlooked during the 1970s, critical and popular interest revived in the late 1980s, leading to major retrospectives and permanent installations at museums worldwide.
Open about her struggles with mental illness, Kusama voluntarily resided in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital from 1977 until her death, crediting art as her primary means of coping with her condition. "I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art", she told an interviewer in 2012. "I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live."

Life and career


Early life: 1929–1949
Yayoi Kusama was born on 22 March 1929 in Matsumoto, Nagano. Born into a merchant family that owned a plant nursery and seed farm, Kusama began drawing pumpkins in elementary school and depicting imagery from her visual hallucinations—motifs that would later define her career. Her mother was not supportive of her creative endeavors; Kusama would rush to finish her art because her mother would take it away to discourage her. Her mother was physically abusive, and she remembered her father as "the type who would play around, who would womanize a lot". She said her mother would often send her to spy on her father's extramarital affairs, which instilled in her a lifelong aversion to sexuality, particularly the male body and the phallus: "I don't like sex. I had an obsession with sex. When I was a child, my father had lovers and I experienced seeing him. My mother sent me to spy on him. I didn't want to have sex with anyone for years ... grok_lead: Yayoi Kusama (22 March 1929 â 14 August 2026) was a Japanese avant-garde artist, painter, sculptor, and author whose oeuvre is defined by obsessive repetition of motifs such as polka dots, nets, and pumpkins, manifesting in paintings, installations, and environmental works that evoke infinity and obliteration. Born in Matsumoto, Nagano Prefecture, into a family operating a seed nursery, Kusama commenced artistic production around age ten, employing polka dots and nets to depict hallucinatory visions of proliferating patterns that engulfed her surroundings. She trained in traditional Nihonga painting before relocating to New York City in 1958, immersing herself in the avant-garde milieu and producing accumulative sculptures and infinity net canvases that intersected with emerging pop art and minimalism. Returning to Japan in the 1970s amid mental health challenges, she resided voluntarily in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital from 1977 until her death, sustaining a voluminous output including mirrored immersion rooms and collaborations with commercial entities like Louis Vuitton. Kusama's recognition escalated in the 21st century with global retrospectives and awards such as the Praemium Imperiale, though her legacy includes scrutiny over passages in her writings portraying Black individuals negatively, prompting a public expression of regret in 2023. Kusama died on 14 August 2026 at a hospital in Tokyo of multiple organ failure.
